madison.intro: Madison's record trees mostly come with paperwork. The University of Wisconsin Arboretum bought a black tupelo for forty cents in 1956 and wrote down the day it was planted out; a blue ash nearby went into the ground on 4 November 1968 and is still alive because it is treated against emerald ash borer. On campus stand Wisconsin's champion pin oak and a ponderosa pine from the far West. In the Vilas neighbourhood, a hackberry 30 metres tall won the city's first Heritage Tree Award for history. All five are free to see.
madison.meta_description: Madison's champion trees: a forty-cent tupelo, a blue ash kept alive against the ash borer, Wisconsin's biggest pin oak and a 30-metre heritage hackberry.
madison.question_meta: Madison's oldest tree we map is the Oakland Avenue hackberry, over a century old by a family account. Its story, and four state champions.
madison.question_answer: The oldest tree we map in Madison is the Oakland Avenue Hackberry in the Vilas neighbourhood, which the family who nominated it say was planted over a hundred years ago by the man who had the first house in the Oakland development built, in 1897. It stands on the city terrace at Oakland Avenue and Madison Street and is also Wisconsin's champion hackberry, 30.2 metres tall.
madison.question_context: Madison's trees are unusually well documented, and the documents mostly describe planted trees rather than ancient ones. The University of Wisconsin Arboretum keeps the life story of its black tupelo down to the day: bought as a seedling for forty cents in 1956, grown on in the nursery, planted out on 3 October 1961. Its blue ash went into the ground on 4 November 1968, grown from seed of a Morton Arboretum tree. Those dates make them about seventy and about sixty, young for record trees, and both species are rare in Wisconsin, wild in one county each. The pin oak in Camp Randall Memorial Park and the ponderosa pine in Allen Centennial Garden have no published age at all. The state's champion register measures size, not years, and a university plant tag reading 56-1527 is a filing number until someone shows it is a date. That leaves the Oakland Avenue hackberry as the oldest, on the strength of a family's account rather than a record, somewhere between about a hundred and 129 years. If you know better, tell us.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Madison?
faq.a: The oldest we map is the Oakland Avenue Hackberry, which the nominating family say was planted over a hundred years ago by the owner of the first house in the Oakland development, built in 1897. That is a family account, so its age sits somewhere between about 100 and 129 years.

faq.q: Are the University of Wisconsin Arboretum trees free to visit?
faq.a: Yes. The Arboretum grounds are free and open from 4 a.m. to 10 p.m., with free parking at the Visitor Center. The champion black tupelo stands at the Visitor Center's north-west corner and the champion blue ash in the ash collection of Longenecker Gardens.

faq.q: Where is Wisconsin's champion pin oak?
faq.a: In Camp Randall Memorial Park on the University of Wisconsin campus, the south-west one of three oaks in the centre of the park, near the Civil War cannon on North Randall Avenue. The state register gives it a trunk 3.94 metres round and a crown about 30 metres wide.

faq.q: Why is the Arboretum's blue ash still alive?
faq.a: The Arboretum treats it against emerald ash borer, the beetle that kills ash. It is one of three ash trees in Longenecker Gardens kept under treatment, and the biggest blue ash in Wisconsin's champion register.

milwaukee.intro: Milwaukee's biggest trees grow on its East Side and in its parks. A street elm 4.91 metres round on North Prospect Avenue is one of the largest American elms left in Wisconsin, seemingly untouched by Dutch elm disease. Lake Park, planned by the Olmsted firm from 1889, keeps oaks its Friends put at 190 to over 200 years old, and a rare English elm. McGovern Park holds the state's champion chinkapin oak, and Forest Home Cemetery a southern overcup oak a long way from home. All six are free.
milwaukee.meta_description: Milwaukee's remarkable trees: a 4.91-metre street elm, Lake Park oaks older than the park, and state champion oaks in McGovern Park and Forest Home.
milwaukee.question_meta: Milwaukee's oldest tree we map is Lake Park's big white oak, over 200 years old by the park Friends' estimate. Its story, and five more.
milwaukee.question_answer: The oldest tree we map in Milwaukee is the big white oak in the Locust Street ravine of Lake Park, which the Lake Park Friends estimated in 2016 at over 200 years old. Close behind are two swamp white oaks just south of the park's tennis courts, put at about 190 years by the same tree walk.
milwaukee.question_context: Milwaukee's oldest trees may be the ones a park was built around. Lake Park sits on ground where, by the Friends' history, Gustav Lueddemann kept the northern forest intact from 1849, and the Olmsted firm began planning the park in 1889. The Friends' printed tree walk dates the park's remnants of native forest to before 1835, and it estimates its biggest white oak at over 200 years and a pair of swamp white oaks at about 190. Those are their estimates, not ring counts, and the book is from 2016, so we say both. Elsewhere the city's record trees are dated by nobody. The Prospect Avenue elm, the McGovern Park chinkapin oak and the overcup oak in Forest Home Cemetery are champions in Wisconsin's state register, which measures girth, height and crown and never asks how old a tree is. A big tree is not automatically an old one, and for the elm nobody has published a figure. If you know one, tell us.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Milwaukee?
faq.a: The oldest we map is the big white oak in Lake Park's Locust Street ravine, estimated by the Lake Park Friends in 2016 at over 200 years old. It is their estimate, not a ring count, and no source since has confirmed it.

faq.q: Is the Prospect Avenue elm the largest American elm in Wisconsin?
faq.a: It may be. A state tree hunter told Wisconsin Public Radio in 2024 it is the champion or co-champion with a Waukesha elm of about the same size, and Urban Milwaukee calls it believed to be the largest surviving American elm in the state. An older list names a Wauwatosa elm instead, so we call it a state champion.

faq.q: Are Milwaukee's remarkable trees free to visit?
faq.a: Yes. Lake Park and McGovern Park are public parks, the Prospect Avenue elm is a street tree seen from the sidewalk, and Forest Home Cemetery is open daily for self-guided visits from 7.30am to 7pm.

richard-bong-state-recreation-area.intro: One tree brings us to Richard Bong State Recreation Area in Kenosha County, and it came from Louisiana. A farmer, John Rhodes, brought a bald cypress north in the 1800s and planted it by his farmhouse. The farm later became Bong Air Base, and the base land became this recreation area, where the cypress still stands by the access road beside a white ash, an Austrian pine and a ginkgo. A 2005 book called it well over 140 years old. The area is open 6am to 11pm and needs a vehicle admission sticker.
richard-bong-state-recreation-area.meta_description: The Rhodes Bald Cypress, brought north from Louisiana in the 1800s, now stands in Richard Bong State Recreation Area, Kenosha County, Wisconsin.
richard-bong-state-recreation-area.question_meta: The oldest tree we map here is the Rhodes Bald Cypress, over 160 years old by a 2005 book's reckoning, brought from Louisiana by a farmer.
richard-bong-state-recreation-area.question_answer: The oldest tree we map in Richard Bong State Recreation Area is the Rhodes Bald Cypress, which a 2005 book called well over 140 years old, putting it past 160 today. John Rhodes brought it north from Estherwood, Louisiana, and planted it by his farmhouse in the mid-1800s.
richard-bong-state-recreation-area.question_context: This is a southern swamp tree living a long way north. The book Every Root an Anchor, published by the Wisconsin Historical Society in 2005, tells its story: brought from Estherwood, Louisiana, planted by the Rhodes farmhouse, then 65 feet tall and 11 feet 5 inches round, and the largest bald cypress in Wisconsin. Its trunk cracked audibly in hard winters and healed over, leaving ridges. A 1962 Wisconsin Historical Society photo caption dates the transplanting to the mid-1800s. Since then the farm has become an air base and the air base a state recreation area, and the cypress has kept its place among a small group of marked champion trees by the access road. The state's champion register now gives it 3.51 metres round and 25 metres tall, figures so close to the book's that the register may carry the old measurement. We found no recent photograph, and the recreation area's own pages do not mention the tree, so if you visit, tell us it is there.

faq.q: How old is the Rhodes Bald Cypress?
faq.a: A 2005 book, Every Root an Anchor, called it well over 140 years old, which puts it past 160 now. A 1962 Wisconsin Historical Society caption says it was transplanted from Louisiana in the mid-1800s. Nobody has published an upper limit.

faq.q: Do you need to pay to visit Richard Bong State Recreation Area?
faq.a: Cars need a vehicle admission sticker, according to the Wisconsin DNR. The area is open from 6am to 11pm all year, and it is reached by car only.

faq.q: Where in the recreation area is the cypress?
faq.a: East of the access road among a group of marked champion trees, with a white ash, an Austrian pine and a ginkgo. Look for the healed frost cracks ridging its trunk.

monroe-wisconsin.intro: Monroe has two of Wisconsin's champion trees standing a few steps apart at Greenwood Cemetery. In front of the cemetery office grows a white fir, a western species planted far from home, 25.6 metres tall with blue-grey needles. Just west of the same office stands a tulip tree 28.2 metres tall, the biggest of its kind in the state register. Neither has a published age, so Monroe's case is size, and the convenience of two records in one stop. Monroe is about 45 minutes by car south-west of Madison.
monroe-wisconsin.meta_description: Two Wisconsin champion trees side by side at Greenwood Cemetery in Monroe: a western white fir and a 28-metre tulip tree.
monroe-wisconsin.question_meta: No tree we map in Monroe has a published age. The biggest is the Greenwood Cemetery tulip tree, Wisconsin's champion at 28.2 metres.
monroe-wisconsin.question_answer: No tree we map in Monroe, Wisconsin has a published age. The biggest is the tulip tree just west of the Greenwood Cemetery office, which Wisconsin's champion register ranks first of its species, 3.18 metres round and 28.2 metres tall.
monroe-wisconsin.question_context: Both of Monroe's record trees stand by the office of Greenwood Cemetery, and both are known from one source only, the Wisconsin DNR champion tree register. That register records girth, height and crown, adds them into a score, and says nothing about age, so neither the tulip tree nor the white fir can be dated from it. The white fir is a western tree, which means somebody planted it here, but the register does not say who or when. The tulip tree is the taller and the heavier of the two, 28.2 metres tall and 3.18 metres round against the fir's 25.6 and 2.62. Its leaves are cut off square at the tip, and in October they turn a clear yellow, which makes autumn the time to come. The register does not record when it measured either tree, so the figures may be some years old. Greenwood is a working cemetery owned by its association; visit in daylight. If you know when either tree was planted, tell us.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Monroe, Wisconsin?
faq.a: Nobody has published an age for either tree we map in Monroe. The biggest is the Greenwood Cemetery tulip tree, the Wisconsin champion of its species at 28.2 metres tall.

faq.q: Where are Monroe's champion trees?
faq.a: Both are at Greenwood Cemetery, by the cemetery office. The white fir stands in front of the office and the tulip tree just west of it.

faq.q: When is the best time to see them?
faq.a: October, when the tulip tree's leaves turn a clear yellow. The white fir keeps its blue-grey needles all year.

la-crosse.intro: La Crosse named a trail after a tree. The Cottonwood Trail through the La Crosse River Marsh takes its name from an eastern cottonwood 7.92 metres round and 29.6 metres tall, the champion of its species in Wisconsin's state register. The marsh trails start from Myrick Park, a city park about ten minutes' drive from downtown, and the Cottonwood Trail is unpaved and free. The tree has no published age, but a visitor recorded it standing at the end of October 2026.
la-crosse.meta_description: La Crosse's Cottonwood Trail is named after its tree: an eastern cottonwood 7.92 metres round in the La Crosse River Marsh, Wisconsin's champion.
la-crosse.question_meta: No tree we map in La Crosse has a published age. The biggest is the cottonwood the Cottonwood Trail is named after, 7.92 metres round.
la-crosse.question_answer: No tree we map in La Crosse has a published age. The biggest is the Cottonwood Trail Giant in the La Crosse River Marsh, an eastern cottonwood 7.92 metres round and 29.6 metres tall, which Wisconsin's champion register ranks first of its species and which gave the Cottonwood Trail its name.
la-crosse.question_context: The Wisconsin DNR champion register scores a tree by adding its trunk in inches, its height in feet and a quarter of its crown, and the La Crosse cottonwood comes to 432 points, the highest score of any Wisconsin tree we map. It earns them almost entirely through its trunk, 312 inches round. The register's history note records that the public trail passing the tree is named after it. What the register does not record is the tree's age, or when it was measured, and nobody else we found has published either. A visitor recorded it at the spot at the end of October 2026, so it is standing. The marsh trails start from Myrick Park, a city park, and the Cottonwood Trail is unpaved; nobody gives the distance from the entrance to the tree, but a loop of about two kilometres runs through this part of the marsh. If you know how old it is, tell us.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in La Crosse?
faq.a: Nobody has published an age for the tree we map in La Crosse. The biggest is the Cottonwood Trail Giant, an eastern cottonwood 7.92 metres round in the La Crosse River Marsh.

faq.q: How do you get to the Cottonwood Trail Giant?
faq.a: Walk in from Myrick Park, where the La Crosse River Marsh trails begin, and follow the unpaved Cottonwood Trail. The tree stands beside the trail that is named after it.

faq.q: Is it free to visit?
faq.a: Yes. The trail is a free public trail in the La Crosse River Marsh, reached from a city park.

fond-du-lac.intro: Wisconsin's champion sycamore grows downtown in Fond du Lac, next to the post office, and it is wider than it is tall. The state's champion register gives it a trunk 6.48 metres round, a height of 25.3 metres and a crown about 31 metres across, with the mottled white bark of its kind. It stands in the town centre rather than a park or a forest, so you can see it from the street, though its exact spot still wants confirming.
fond-du-lac.meta_description: Wisconsin's champion sycamore stands next to the post office in downtown Fond du Lac: a trunk 6.48 metres round under a 31-metre crown.
fond-du-lac.question_meta: No tree we map in Fond du Lac has a published age. The biggest is the downtown sycamore, Wisconsin's champion, 6.48 metres round.
fond-du-lac.question_answer: No tree we map in Fond du Lac has a published age. The biggest is the sycamore next to the post office downtown, which Wisconsin's champion register ranks first of its species, with a trunk 6.48 metres round and a crown about 31 metres across.
fond-du-lac.question_context: Fond du Lac's record tree is known from a single source, the Wisconsin DNR champion register, and that source is thin. It places the sycamore in the city of Fond du Lac next to the post office, without naming which post office, and it gives no measurement date and no age. A visitor recorded a sycamore near the register's point in July 2023, which is the most recent sign of life we have. What the register does give is the size. Its crown spreads about 31 metres one way and 26.5 the other on a tree 25.3 metres high, and its trunk is 6.48 metres round, well over half again as thick as the champion sycamore of Chicago's forest preserves, which is 3.91 metres round but much taller. We read the tree as one you see from the street, on the public side, but our pin is approximate. If you walk past it, tell us exactly where it stands, and if you know its age, tell us that too.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Fond du Lac?
faq.a: Nobody has published an age for the tree we map in Fond du Lac. The biggest is the sycamore next to the downtown post office, Wisconsin's champion of its species.

faq.q: Where exactly is the champion sycamore?
faq.a: The state register says next to the post office in the city of Fond du Lac, without naming the building. Our pin is downtown and approximate; look for mottled white bark and a crown about 31 metres across.

faq.q: Can you visit it?
faq.a: It reads as a street-side tree seen from public ground, so it costs nothing to look at. Street parking is available downtown.

platteville.intro: On the University of Wisconsin-Platteville campus, thirty yards south of the library, Wisconsin's champion northern catalpa holds up one of its own limbs on concrete blocks. The state register gives it a trunk 6.71 metres round, measured low because it splits about a metre up, a height of 28 metres and a crown about 24 metres across. The register's curator re-measured it in August 2021 and found its foliage still full. Platteville is about an hour and a quarter by car south-west of Madison.
platteville.meta_description: Wisconsin's champion catalpa grows south of the library at UW-Platteville, 6.71 metres round, with its big west bough propped on concrete blocks.
platteville.question_meta: No tree we map in Platteville has a published age. The biggest is the campus catalpa, Wisconsin's champion, with a bough propped on blocks.
platteville.question_answer: No tree we map in Platteville has a published age. The biggest is the northern catalpa thirty yards south of the library on the University of Wisconsin-Platteville campus, which Wisconsin's champion register ranks first of its species, 6.71 metres round and 28 metres tall.
platteville.question_context: The best account of Platteville's catalpa is a short note from the state champion register's curator, dated 25 August 2021. It describes an old champion re-measured, its trunk splitting between one and one and a half metres above the ground, its foliage still full, and its large west bough supported on concrete blocks. Because of the split, the diameter was taken at 36 inches rather than at the usual height, so the register's 6.71 metres round is best read as approximate. The register gives the tree a height of 28 metres and a crown about 24 metres one way and 22.5 the other, and scores it at 375 points, but it records no age, and nobody else we found has published one. That 2021 note is also the most recent confirmation that the tree is alive. The campus lawn has no gate we know of, though we have not confirmed access. If you study or work at the university and know when the catalpa was planted, tell us.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Platteville?
faq.a: Nobody has published an age for the tree we map in Platteville. The biggest is the northern catalpa south of the UW-Platteville library, Wisconsin's champion of its species.

faq.q: Why is the catalpa's branch on concrete blocks?
faq.a: Its large west bough is supported on concrete blocks, as the state register's curator recorded when re-measuring the tree in August 2021. The trunk splits low, between one and one and a half metres above the ground.

faq.q: Where on campus is it?
faq.a: Thirty yards south of the library on the University of Wisconsin-Platteville campus.

poynette.intro: Near Poynette, the MacKenzie Environmental Education Center keeps three of Wisconsin's champion trees within a couple of hundred metres of each other: a yellow buckeye north of the office, a sweet birch with a crown nearly as wide as it is tall, and a chestnut oak growing outside its natural range. All three were planted. The centre began as the State Game Farm and took its present name in 1971. It is about 40 minutes by car north of Madison; check hours before you go.
poynette.meta_description: Three Wisconsin champion trees in one arboretum near Poynette: a yellow buckeye, a sweet birch and a chestnut oak at the MacKenzie Center.
poynette.question_meta: No tree we map at Poynette has a published age. The biggest is the MacKenzie Center's yellow buckeye, Wisconsin's champion.
poynette.question_answer: No tree we map near Poynette has a published age. The biggest of the three is the yellow buckeye at the MacKenzie Environmental Education Center, west of the sidewalk and north of the office, which Wisconsin's champion register ranks first of its species, 2.26 metres round and 22.6 metres tall.
poynette.question_context: The MacKenzie Center's arboretum is a planted collection, and its three register champions are planted trees, the chestnut oak well outside its natural range. None of the three is enormous. The buckeye is 22.6 metres tall, the birch 21.3, the oak 20.1, and their trunks run from 1.78 to 2.26 metres round. What they offer is a short walk past three state records, from the buckeye near the office west to the birch and the chestnut oak at the far side of the arboretum. The register lists the buckeye under an older botanical name, Aesculus octandra, now a synonym of Aesculus flava. It is the only source for all three trees and records neither measurement dates nor ages, and the arboretum's planting dates are not published anywhere we found. The site itself has a history, as the State Game Farm until it was renamed in 1971. Visiting hours and any fee were not confirmed, so check with the centre first. If you know when the arboretum was planted, tell us.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree at Poynette?
faq.a: Nobody has published an age for any of the three trees we map at the MacKenzie Center. The biggest is the yellow buckeye north of the office, Wisconsin's champion of its species.

faq.q: Which champion trees grow at the MacKenzie Center?
faq.a: Three, by the Wisconsin DNR register: a yellow buckeye north of the office, a sweet birch at the west end of the western part of the arboretum, and a chestnut oak west of the conservation exhibit. All three were planted.

faq.q: Is the MacKenzie Center open to visitors?
faq.a: It is a state-run environmental education centre with a planted arboretum. We could not confirm its hours or whether there is a fee, so check with the centre before the drive.

eagle-wisconsin.intro: Near Eagle, by the headquarters of the Kettle Moraine State Forest, stands Wisconsin's champion black cherry, 32 metres tall with a trunk 2.74 metres round and a crown about 20 metres across. The state register says to park at the headquarters lot and use the walking paths. Its coordinates are rounded, so the building is the best guide. It is about 50 minutes by car south-west of Milwaukee, and a vehicle admission sticker is likely needed in the state forest.
eagle-wisconsin.meta_description: Wisconsin's champion black cherry, 32 metres tall, grows by the Kettle Moraine State Forest headquarters near Eagle.
eagle-wisconsin.question_meta: No tree we map near Eagle has a published age. The biggest is Kettle Moraine's black cherry, Wisconsin's champion at 32 metres.
eagle-wisconsin.question_answer: No tree we map near Eagle, Wisconsin has a published age. The biggest is the black cherry by the Kettle Moraine State Forest headquarters, which Wisconsin's champion register ranks first of its species, 32 metres tall and 2.74 metres round.
eagle-wisconsin.question_context: The Kettle Moraine black cherry is a register tree, known from the Wisconsin DNR champion list and nothing else we found. The register names it only as near the Kettle Moraine headquarters, in Waukesha County; we read that as the Southern Unit's headquarters near Eagle, which the register itself does not confirm, and its coordinates carry only three decimals, so our pin is loose. The register gives it a height of 32 metres, 105 feet, a trunk 2.74 metres round and a crown about 20 metres across in both directions, close to a circle. That height matters more than the girth here. The champion black cherry of Chicago's forest preserves is thicker, 3.35 metres round, but 29.3 metres tall, while a second-ranked one in Swallow Cliff Woods reaches 34.7. Champion registers score the whole tree, so the tallest does not always win. The register gives no measurement date and no age. If you have seen the tree, or know how old it is, tell us.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree near Eagle, Wisconsin?
faq.a: Nobody has published an age for the tree we map near Eagle. The biggest is the black cherry by the Kettle Moraine State Forest headquarters, Wisconsin's champion of its species.

faq.q: How do you find the Kettle Moraine black cherry?
faq.a: The state register says to park at the headquarters lot and use the walking paths; the tree is near the headquarters building. Our pin is approximate.

faq.q: Do you need to pay to visit?
faq.a: A vehicle admission sticker is likely needed for cars in the Kettle Moraine State Forest. We have not confirmed it for this lot.

solon-springs.intro: In Lucius Woods County Park at Solon Springs, at the south-west corner of the car park, stands Wisconsin's champion red pine, 34.2 metres tall with plated orange-brown bark. That is nearly 15 metres taller than the state champion red pine of Illinois. The park lies on Upper St. Croix Lake and is open to day visitors, with a beach, a campground and a nature trail. Solon Springs is about 35 minutes by car south-east of Superior.
solon-springs.meta_description: Wisconsin's champion red pine, 34.2 metres tall, stands by the car park in Lucius Woods County Park, Solon Springs, on Upper St. Croix Lake.
solon-springs.question_meta: No tree we map in Solon Springs has a published age. The biggest is the Lucius Woods red pine, Wisconsin's champion at 34.2 metres.
solon-springs.question_answer: No tree we map in Solon Springs has a published age. The biggest is the red pine at the south-west corner of the car park in Lucius Woods County Park, which Wisconsin's champion register ranks first of its species, 34.2 metres tall and 2.63 metres round.
solon-springs.question_context: Solon Springs' record tree is easy to reach. The Wisconsin DNR champion register puts the Lucius Woods red pine at the south-west corner of the parking lot in the middle of the park, and the register file even holds a hand-drawn map. It measured a trunk 2.63 metres round and a height of 34.2 metres, 112 feet, under a narrow crown about 12 metres across. For comparison, the state champion red pine of Illinois, on a golf course on our Chicago page, is 19.5 metres tall and 2.07 metres round. Lucius Woods is a Douglas County park on Upper St. Croix Lake, open to day visitors, and as far as we found the fees are for camping only. The register is the only source for the tree itself. It does not say when it took its measurements and does not give an age, and nobody else we found has dated it. If you camp or swim here and know more about the pine, tell us.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Solon Springs?
faq.a: Nobody has published an age for the tree we map in Solon Springs. The biggest is the Lucius Woods red pine, Wisconsin's champion of its species at 34.2 metres tall.

faq.q: Where is the champion red pine in Lucius Woods County Park?
faq.a: At the south-west corner of the parking lot in the middle of the park. Look for plated orange-brown bark on a tall, narrow-crowned pine.

faq.q: Does Lucius Woods County Park charge entry?
faq.a: As far as we found, fees apply to camping only; the park is open to day visitors.

nicolet-national-forest.intro: In the Nicolet National Forest in Forest County, an eastern white pine stands 47.9 metres tall, 157 feet by the Wisconsin champion register, beside a gravel forest road. It is east of Forest Road 2454, Huff Creek Road, and can be seen from the road itself. The trunk is 3.96 metres round. It stands on US Forest Service land, free to visit, but remote, with no public transport, and forest roads like this one can close for the season.
nicolet-national-forest.meta_description: A 47.9-metre eastern white pine, Wisconsin's champion, seen from Huff Creek Road in the Nicolet National Forest, Forest County.
nicolet-national-forest.question_meta: No tree we map in the Nicolet National Forest has a published age. The biggest is the Huff Creek Road white pine, 47.9 metres tall.
nicolet-national-forest.question_answer: No tree we map in the Nicolet National Forest has a published age. The biggest is the Huff Creek Road White Pine, east of Forest Road 2454 in Forest County, which Wisconsin's champion register ranks first of its species, 47.9 metres tall and 3.96 metres round.
nicolet-national-forest.question_context: The Huff Creek Road pine is a register tree, and the Wisconsin DNR champion list is the only source we have for it. It records a height of 157 feet, 47.9 metres, a trunk 3.96 metres round and a crown about 16 metres one way and 15 the other, and it says the tree is visible from Huff Creek Road, to the east. The height is the register's measurement, not ours, and the register does not say when it was taken. To give that number some scale, the champion white pine of Chicago's forest preserves is 29.3 metres tall, so this one stands more than 18 metres higher. Its crown is narrow for its height, barely a third as wide as the tree is tall. The forest is US Forest Service land and free to visit, but the road is gravel and may close seasonally, and the nearest towns are some way off. Nobody has published an age for the pine. If you know it, or have seen the tree recently, tell us.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in the Nicolet National Forest?
faq.a: Nobody has published an age for the tree we map there. The biggest is the Huff Creek Road White Pine, Wisconsin's champion eastern white pine at 47.9 metres tall.

faq.q: Can you see the Huff Creek Road pine without hiking?
faq.a: Yes. The state register says it is visible from Huff Creek Road, Forest Road 2454, standing to the east of the road.

faq.q: Is the road open all year?
faq.a: It is a gravel forest road, and forest roads can close for the season, so check with the Forest Service before you drive.

florence-county-wisconsin.intro: On the Assessor's Interpretive Trail by Lost Lake in Florence County, a sign marks a tree as a basswood. Wisconsin's champion register adds that it is the biggest basswood in the state, 36.6 metres tall and 4.09 metres round. The trail starts at the east end of the lake beside the campground in the Chequamegon-Nicolet National Forest and runs through hemlocks and hardwoods past interpretive signs and a named white pine. It is free, remote and reached by car.
florence-county-wisconsin.meta_description: Wisconsin's champion basswood, 36.6 metres tall, on the Assessor's Interpretive Trail by Lost Lake in Florence County.
florence-county-wisconsin.question_meta: No tree we map in Florence County has a published age. The biggest is the Assessor's Trail basswood, Wisconsin's champion at 36.6 metres.
florence-county-wisconsin.question_answer: No tree we map in Florence County, Wisconsin has a published age. The biggest is the American basswood on the Assessor's Interpretive Trail by Lost Lake, which Wisconsin's champion register ranks first of its species, 36.6 metres tall and 4.09 metres round.
florence-county-wisconsin.question_context: Florence County's record tree comes with two sources that agree on where it is. The Wisconsin DNR champion register measures the basswood at 161 inches round, 4.09 metres, and 120 feet tall, 36.6 metres, with a crown about 21 metres across, and says a sign marks it on the trail. The US Forest Service describes the trail itself, the Assessor's Interpretive Trail at the east end of Lost Lake beside the campground, through hemlocks and hardwoods, with interpretive signs and a named tree of its own, the Assessor White Pine. Set beside the champion basswood of Chicago's forest preserves, 3.91 metres round and 24.4 metres tall, this one is a little thicker and twelve metres taller. The register gives no measurement date, and nobody has published an age for the tree. The trail is free, there is no public transport, and Florence is the nearest town to drive from. If you walk it and know the basswood's age, or see it on the way, tell us.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Florence County, Wisconsin?
faq.a: Nobody has published an age for the tree we map there. The biggest is the basswood on the Assessor's Interpretive Trail, Wisconsin's champion of its species at 36.6 metres tall.

faq.q: Where is the Assessor's Interpretive Trail?
faq.a: At the east end of Lost Lake, beside the Lost Lake Campground in the Chequamegon-Nicolet National Forest, according to the US Forest Service.

faq.q: How do you know which tree is the champion basswood?
faq.a: The state register says a sign on the trail marks it as a basswood. It is 36.6 metres tall and 4.09 metres round.

chicago.intro: Chicago is a young city on old prairie, and its oldest trees are the prairie's survivors: bur oaks that stood here before the city had a name. One shaded the Midway while the 1893 World's Fair rose around it, and a Norwood Park savanna remnant may be older than the United States. The county's forest preserves hold ranked champions: a sycamore and a cottonwood both 41.5 metres tall, a walnut with a 31-metre crown, oaks of seven kinds. The famous zoo oak fell in 2023. Forty-one of the forty-three are free; the two golf-course champions generally need a green fee.
chicago.meta_description: Chicago's remarkable trees: prairie bur oaks older than the city, and Cook County's forest preserve champions, from 40-metre cottonwoods to white oaks.
chicago.question_meta: Chicago's oldest trees are the bur oaks of Union Ridge Cemetery, estimated at 325 to 375 years. Their story, and 42 more remarkable trees.
chicago.question_answer: Chicago's oldest known trees are the bur oaks of the Union Ridge Cemetery savanna in Norwood Park, estimated by one expert survey at 325 to 375 years, older than the United States. The most storied is the bur oak on the Midway Plaisance in Hyde Park, which stood before the 1893 World's Fair was laid out around it.
chicago.question_context: Chicago's relationship with old trees is mostly a story of what the prairie kept. The city itself is young, incorporated in 1837, and it burned in 1871, so almost nothing planted stands out for age. What survives is what was already here, the bur oaks, the prairie's fire-resistant veterans, in the few corners the city never quite got around to flattening. The best known of them, the bur oak at Lincoln Park Zoo that generations called Chicago's oldest tree, was cut down in May 2023 after it died, which quietly promoted the others. The Midway oak in Hyde Park carries a genuine dispute, one university account says it was planted for the 1893 fair, others say the fair was built around it, and its page gives both versions. The Union Ridge savanna's ages rest on a single expert's estimate and say so, as does a bur oak on Northwestern's campus in Evanston, put at perhaps 250 years by the university's landscape architect. The register Illinois keeps for its champion trees records size, not age, and so does the county's own; a champion is not automatically ancient.

faq_update.q: Are Chicago's remarkable trees free to visit?
faq_update.a: Forty-one of the forty-three are free. The Midway oak and the Wooded Island grove stand in public parks, Union Ridge is a cemetery open in daylight hours, the forest preserve champions stand on public preserve land, and the Evanston bur oak stands on Northwestern University's grounds beside Sheridan Road. The champion boxelder and the champion red pine stand on public golf courses, where a green fee is generally needed to walk the course; ask at the clubhouse.

faq_add.q: Is a Cook County champion always the tallest tree of its kind?
faq_add.a: No. The Forest Preserves of Cook County score a tree by adding its trunk in inches, its height in feet and a quarter of its crown, so a thick trunk can outscore a tall one. Their second-ranked black cherry, in Swallow Cliff Woods, is 34.7 metres tall, 5.4 metres taller than the champion at Camp Ground Road Woods, and both the second and third-ranked pin oaks are taller than the champion at Rolling Knolls.

faq_add.q: Is there an old tree at Northwestern University in Evanston?
faq_add.a: Yes. Just east of 1835 Hinman, across Sheridan Road from Fisk Hall, stands a bur oak the university's landscape architect put at perhaps 250 years in 2018. She reads its horizontal branches as a sign that it survives from the oak savanna at the south end of the campus. It is an estimate, not a ring count.
